profile.name: Reajul Islam Robin
profile.focus: Distributed Systems · Concurrency & Consistency · Payments · Healthcare
profile.headline: I build backend systems that stay correct under concurrency, retries and failure — from race-free booking to forgery-safe payments.
profile.summary: I'm a backend engineer in Dhaka building distributed systems for healthcare and fintech. Most of my work lives where correctness is non-negotiable: scarce appointment slots, payments, and medical records. I like problems that look simple until two requests arrive at once — and I prove the answers with tests that actually race. Before healthcare I built PCI-DSS-aligned payment APIs for a fintech payments platform.
profile.education: B.Sc.(Engg.) Computer Science & Engineering · Mawlana Bhashani Science & Technology University (2017–2021)
profile.credibility: Backend engineer · .NET & PostgreSQL · 3 years building distributed systems for healthcare and payments

experience.summary: Designed and built the appointment, payment and telemedicine services of a national telehealth platform — .NET 8 microservices with Clean Architecture and CQRS on PostgreSQL.

achievements.detail: Slot-hold lifecycle with a 5-minute hold, a fresh 10-minute payment window and eight convergent release paths; first-come-first-served enforced by a partial unique index, row-version optimistic concurrency and Postgres advisory locks, proven by real-database race tests (8 concurrent patients → 1 booking).

Extracted SSLCommerz into its own service; every callback re-validated with the provider, validity and ownership reported as separate signals so a forged callback can't release another patient's slot, and layered idempotency (natural keys, unique-index backstops, receiver dedupe).
Appointment-scoped Agora video, signalling and screen-share tokens with server-derived channels, party and join-window checks, and expiry pinned to the end of the slot.

achievements.lead: Turned consultations into an encrypted medical record
achievements.detail: Append-only, undeletable transcripts encrypted with AES-256-GCM (purpose-bound, key rotation), PHI-safe logging verified by tests, event-driven sealing re-verified at the source, and LLM-generated summaries for long calls.

achievements.lead: Built reliable messaging without losing atomicity
achievements.detail: Transactional outbox with per-channel delivery semantics, backoff and dead-lettering; Kafka-ready event contracts; live availability over SSE fanned out with Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY.

Docker and Kubernetes (K3s) deployments via GitLab CI, Kafka and RabbitMQ operations — including diagnosing a disk-space incident on Kafka's storage volume — with Graylog logging and OpenTelemetry/Zipkin tracing.

experience.summary: Built PCI-DSS-aligned ASP.NET Core payment APIs on SQL Server for ConnexPay, a fintech payments platform.

achievements.detail: Secure, high-throughput ASP.NET Core Web APIs with Microsoft Identity authentication, role-based authorization and consistent error handling.
Visa, TSYS and BlueSnap — webhook/IPN handling, transaction validation and ledger updates.

projects.name: SNOMED CT Clinical Search API
projects.description: A clinical-terminology search API over the SNOMED CT release: word-order-independent ranked search with a trigram fuzzy fallback, concept details, and IS-A hierarchy browsing — written directly against PostgreSQL.
highlights: Word-order-independent search: every query word must appear in a description, results ranked exact → prefix → contains and then by term length, and deduplicated to one row per concept with DISTINCT ON.
Typo tolerance without a search engine: when nothing matches, the query falls back to pg_trgm trigram similarity (the % operator with a 0.3 similarity floor), ranked by score.

Clinically sensible results: only active concepts and descriptions, filtered by semantic tag (findings by default, for chief complaints), with the shortest active synonym chosen as the preferred term.
Hierarchy browsing over SNOMED's IS-A relationships — parents, children and child counts — so a UI can drill from a symptom down to more specific findings.
A paged search endpoint with a separate total-count query, plus an interactive console client for exploring concepts and their definitions.

diagrams.title: Search pipeline
diagrams.caption: Every query word must match; results are ranked and collapsed to one row per concept. Only when nothing matches does the query fall back to trigram similarity — so exact intent wins, and typos still find something.

diagrams.title: Architecture
diagrams.caption: A thin ASP.NET Core API and a console client share one repository that issues hand-written SQL against the SNOMED CT release tables — concepts, descriptions, relationships and definitions.

principles.title: Make invariants the database's job
principles.detail: If two requests can race, a check in application code will eventually lose. Uniqueness and ownership rules live in constraints and locks the database enforces.

principles.title: Assume every message arrives twice
principles.detail: Providers retry, clients double-submit, networks duplicate. Every write that matters carries an idempotency key, with a unique index as the backstop.

principles.title: Model lifecycles explicitly; make cleanup converge
principles.detail: State machines with terminal states, and several independent paths to clean up — so a stalled background job can never strand a resource.

principles.title: Trust identifiers, verify everything else
principles.detail: Inbound callbacks and headers are claims, not facts. Re-fetch the truth from its owner and derive access identifiers on the server.

principles.title: Commit state and intent together
principles.detail: A state change and the events it causes are written in one transaction, then delivered with semantics chosen per channel.

principles.title: Prove concurrency with real races
principles.detail: Mocks can't reproduce a race. Tests spin up a real Postgres and send concurrent requests at the same slot, payment or record.

caseStudies.title: Race-free appointment booking
caseStudies.summary: A booking service for a national telehealth platform where patients compete for limited doctor slots — and a slot can never be sold twice, even when payments are slow, fail or call back twice.
caseStudies.problem: Patients race for scarce slots, and every booking waits on an external payment provider that can be slow, fail or deliver its callback twice. A slot must never be sold twice, abandoned checkouts must free slots quickly, and no outcome may depend on a background job running on time.

diagrams.title: Architecture
diagrams.caption: The appointment service owns the booking lifecycle. Postgres enforces first-come-first-served; payment reports outcomes, booking decides; events leave through an outbox written in the same transaction.

diagrams.title: Slot-hold lifecycle
diagrams.caption: A claim holds a slot for 5 minutes; checkout opens a fresh 10-minute payment window. Eight independent paths converge on Expired — lazy expiry on read and reclaim-on-conflict guarantee correctness on their own, so the sweep is only housekeeping.

decisions.choice: Fairness as a database constraint, not application code
decisions.why: Check-then-insert loses races. A partial unique index over doctor, venue, date and start time decides the winner atomically — and writing it exposed a gap in the original key: NULLs never collide in a unique index, so online slots would have been unprotected.

decisions.choice: Row-version optimistic concurrency plus advisory locks
decisions.why: Most conflicts are rare and cheap to retry, so Postgres row versions with bounded retries handle them. Cross-row rules — one live claim per patient per doctor, sequential queue numbers — use transaction-scoped advisory locks, because in-process locks silently break at two replicas.

decisions.choice: Eight convergent ways to release a hold
decisions.why: Lazy expiry on read and reclaim-on-conflict at insert guarantee correctness on their own; a SKIP LOCKED sweep, explicit release, verified payment failure, checkout auto-release, cancel and purge are housekeeping. A stalled job can never strand a slot.

decisions.choice: Reset, don't extend, the payment window
decisions.why: A 5-minute review hold, then a fresh 10-minute window per checkout attempt (max 3) gives patients a predictable deadline and bounds how long a slot can be tied up.
Once the interface has told a patient the slot was lost, a late payment is refunded rather than silently reviving the booking.

Notifications are written in the same transaction as the state change, so a rolled-back booking notifies nobody. Delivery semantics are chosen per channel: at-most-once for SMS and feeds that aren't idempotent, at-least-once for services that dedupe. Contracts are Kafka-ready.

results: 1,052 automated tests, including real-Postgres race tests: eight patients racing for one slot get exactly one booking; a three-seat session gets exactly three; duplicate payment callbacks confirm once and notify once; a payment racing the sweep never confirms an expired hold.
40 API endpoints and 7 background jobs, each single-run across replicas.
Live availability pushed over Server-Sent Events and fanned out across pods with Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY — real-time without adding a broker.
caseStudies.tagline: Slots are never sold twice — even when payments are slow, fail or call back twice.

caseStudies.title: Exactly-once, forgery-safe payments
caseStudies.summary: A payment service that turns an external provider's public, retrying, forgeable callbacks into exactly one trustworthy outcome per booking.
caseStudies.problem: Payment callbacks hit public, unauthenticated routes. They can be duplicated, arrive out of order, or be forged — and the booking must be confirmed exactly once, or released only when the payment genuinely failed.

diagrams.title: Verification flow
diagrams.caption: Callbacks arrive on public routes, so the payment service treats them as claims: it re-fetches the result from the provider, records it idempotently, and reports validity and ownership as two separate signals. The booking service makes the decision.

decisions.choice: Trust lookup keys only; re-fetch the facts
decisions.why: A callback body is attacker-controlled. Only the transaction and validation ids are used, to look the payment up; status and amount are always re-fetched server-to-server from the provider, failing closed if nothing matches.

decisions.choice: Report validity and ownership as two signals
decisions.why: Merging "is the payment valid" with "does it belong to this booking" would let a forged callback — a fake transaction id paired with someone else's real validation id — release another patient's slot. Caught while implementing the service contract.
Only the booking service knows the booking's state and fee, so it makes every state decision. An amount mismatch is flagged for manual reconciliation and the booking is left untouched.

A natural key is checked before writing and backed by a unique index for concurrent duplicates; a violation becomes a typed duplicate that returns 200, so the provider stops retrying. The receiving service dedupes again.
Double clicks and two open tabs must yield one checkout session. A Postgres advisory lock per booking serialises creation across replicas; an existing pending session is reused.

decisions.choice: HTTP plus a retry sweeper instead of a broker
decisions.why: Because the receiver dedupes, outcome delivery can be at-least-once without new infrastructure: a sweeper re-sends unreported outcomes from a partial index, and the provider's callback stays the authoritative path while the browser redirect is a best-effort fast path.

results: 110 tests in the payment service and 44 payment-related tests in the booking service, plus an 11-scenario edge-case suite: double-session races, duplicate and malformed callbacks, retry after decline, cancel-versus-pay.
Extracted from the booking service as a lift-and-shift with no client-visible change, then hardened in place.
Timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers on every outbound call; raw provider payloads kept at every stage for reconciliation.
caseStudies.tagline: Public, retrying, forgeable callbacks become exactly one trusted outcome per booking.

caseStudies.title: Secure video consultations with an encrypted record
caseStudies.summary: A telemedicine service that lets only the booked doctor and patient into a call, only around the appointment, and keeps what was said as an encrypted, append-only medical record with an AI summary.
caseStudies.problem: Only the booked doctor and patient may join, only around the appointment time — and what's said becomes part of a medical record that must be private, tamper-resistant, never leaked through logs, and summarised for follow-up.

figures.label: encrypted at rest, with key rotation

diagrams.title: Access & record
diagrams.caption: Rooms are derived from the appointment, never stored. Tokens are minted only for the booked doctor and patient, inside the join window, and expire at slot end. Transcripts are encrypted, append-only and sealed by the server; a summary is generated once sealed.

decisions.choice: Derive rooms; assign identifiers on the server
decisions.why: The channel and participant ids are computed from the appointment, never taken from the request — nothing to store and nothing to forge. Moving tokens behind the gateway's authentication closed a path where a forged identity header could mint a token for any call.

decisions.choice: A join window tied to the booking
decisions.why: Tokens are issued only to the booking's doctor or patient, from ten minutes before the start until ten minutes after the end, and expire exactly at window close. Clients offer a slightly tighter window to the patient so the doctor arrives first.

When the booking service reports that a visit ended, the transcript is sealed only after re-checking the status at the source — a forged event can't end a live call. Handlers are idempotent instead of needing an inbox table.
Each value carries its key id for rotation, and associated data binds the purpose, so ciphertext moved between columns fails to decrypt. The record is append-only and undeletable in three layers.
Replacing the whole transcript every ten seconds meant hundreds of large rewrites an hour and a risk of truncation. An append endpoint dedupes turns by id and retries cleanly on version races.
Identifiers are logged as short hashes, content is never logged or echoed in errors, and tests assert it — so observability never becomes a leak.

results: 240 automated tests, including real-Postgres tests and assertions that logs never contain patient data.
Consultation summaries generated within minutes of a call ending, with chunked map-reduce summarisation for long conversations.
A focused service: scheduling was moved out to the booking service, leaving telemedicine with one table and no session state.
caseStudies.tagline: Only the booked doctor and patient get in; what's said becomes an encrypted, append-only record.
